Sentinel cells are cells that act as the first line of defence against infection, and therefore are all located in the tissues. They include macrophages, dendritic cells, mast cells, and the nucleated cells of the kidney and liver.  Pathogens are detected by the sentinel cells and if they are found to be microbes, the sentinel cells are activated.  The three main types of sentinel cells are macrophages, dendritic cells and mast cells.  Macrophages are present in all tissues and are the most common type of sentinel cell. Dendritic cells are found in the skin and sub-cutaneous tissue, and migrate to the nearest draining lymph node upon activation. Mast cells are found in the skin and internal visceral organs.  NK cells are cells of the blood, and are not sentinel cells. They are part of the innate immune system, and are important in the defence against viral infection.  Langerhans cells are a type of dendritic cell, found in the epidermis of the skin.

HCN4 channels are hyperpolarised cyclic gated inwardly rectifying potassium channels. Activation of beta adrenergic receptors via noradrenaline causes an increase in cAMP production and therefore an increase in HCN4 channel activity. This would cause a decrease in the strength of the cardiac action potential (end diastolic interval) and therefore a negative chronotropic effect. Ryanodine receptors are the receptors on the SR that are activated by increased Ca2+ movement into the cell. This causes further release of Ca2+ from the SR, causing a stronger contraction (positive inotropic effect).
